item.title: Stand-up comic released after being convicted of insulting Erdoğan
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8zxzlqwzw0eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Stand-up comic released after being convicted of insulting Erdoğan - Published An Istanbul court has convicted a popular comedian of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan – and handed down a sentence of almost 19 months – but ordered his release due to time served. It has also placed him under a travel ban, preventing him from travelling outside Turkey. A final decision in the case will come from the court of appeals. Deniz Göktaş - who denied the charges - has already spent nearly 90 days in prison. Prosecutors had asked for up to 12 years. His case comes amid a wave of arrests in Turkey that human rights groups say is aimed at crushing dissent. His stand-up routine went viral on YouTube, attracting more than 15 million views. Prosecutors had singled out a line in which the comedian called the Turkish leader "a shy dictator", but Göktaş insisted there was "no criminal element" in his comments. "Dictator is not an insult," he said, "it is a political characterisation." But angering the president in Turkey is not funny. Göktaş was arrested and handcuffed at Istanbul airport in July when he returned from a holiday. During his court appearance on Monday, it was clear he did not lose his sense of humour during his 88 days in solitary confinement. "Three months have been taken away from my life," he said on the stand. "But I quit smoking, so I'll add another three months to my life." That drew laughter and loud applause in court. Outside, supporters like Firat Aksal – a fellow comedian – were very pleasantly surprised by the verdict. "We hardly know what to do with our happiness," he said. "We are thrilled. To be honest we weren't hopeful of getting a fair trial. " Göktaş was released at 21:45 local time (18:45 GMT) and greeted by well-wishers, including his parents who he was seen hugging, outside a prison facility. Aksal said Göktaş would now rest for a few days, and see his family, and then return to the stage. After his release, Göktaş told reporters: "I'm very happy to be reunited with my family, mother, father, and friends." But he added: "There are thousands of other people in prisons across Turkey. Some, like me, are being held in pre-trial detention, while others have been convicted because of their views. "So, of course, it's wonderful to be out. I've missed it very much. But there is not much difference between inside and outside. I hope the day comes when we can all regain our freedom together." Many others remain behind bars, including journalists, human rights campaigners, student protesters, LGBTQ activists, and the elected Mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem Imamoglu. Prisons are full in Turkey these days. Erdogan and his party in the past have denied arrests, such as that of Imamoglu, have been politically motivated, insisting that Turkey's judiciary is independent. Additional reporting by Gunce Akpamuk

item.title: The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalry
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c61wxyzr4rwyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalry - Published Snipers shatter the silence of the Australian bush. Then the missiles hit, the smoke rising in the distance. The buzz of drones starts up, soon to be drowned out by helicopters flying overhead. Every piece of hardware is being deployed, no expense spared. But this is no war zone – the last time Townsville saw conflict was during World War Two. This is a show of military might. " We live in a volatile world," says Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan. "Training an army to be prepared to fight a war that is potentially more likely than it has been previously, [is] very important." War is no longer an abstract concept for Australians who often feel removed from the problems facing other parts of the world. Thousands of miles from active conflict, the country, like everywhere else, is facing the knock-on effects of Iran and Ukraine such as higher fuel prices and rising inflation. With China's military capabilities also on the rise and its increasing influence in the Pacific, there's also more concern about the threat it represents. Australia has responded by deepening its relationship with the US, its security ally and China's rival superpower. But that also puts Australia in a tricky position - for China's rise has also given Australia its biggest trading partner. It's a paradox that most people are well aware of - which is probably why we've been invited to report on what Australia is doing to protect itself but nobody is willing to say whom they're preparing to fight. "We're rehearsing for a war - the worst type of war - a World War Two-like war, a World War One-type war, a total war," says Brigadier McLennan, preferring to remain vague when asked who the enemy is. Binding tighter to the US The war scenario playing out before us is part of a major joint exercise known as "Southern Jackaroo" - a training programme involving the Australian, American and Japanese armed forces aimed at strengthening defence co-operation across the Indo-Pacific. "We like to call ourselves America's 911 response force," US Marine Kevin Hicks says. And in terms of numbers, they are more prepared than ever. In 2012, just 200 US Marines were deployed to Australia for an annual six-month deployment. Today, that figure has risen to around 2,500. A quick read of Australia's 2026 National Defence Strategy gives you an easy answer as to why these numbers are growing. "Intense competition between major powers – principally the United States and China – will be an enduring feature of our strategic environment," it said. "China continues to undertake the largest military build-up in the world today, without the transparency or strategic reassurance the region expects." The military tie-ups aren't just being seen in terms of troops but in bases too - most obviously in the north of the country such as RAAF Tindal air base in the Northern Territory which has been upgraded to support long-range American B52 bombers. But the security partnership between the US, the UK and Australia - Aukus - arming Australia with nuclear submarines, is arguably the biggest example of deepening ties. The Australian approach differs from that of its fellow middle powers. While Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has talked about middle powers reorganising their priorities in light of an increasingly unreliable US, Australia seems to be intent on tying itself ever closer. But that comes as Australians themselves increasingly doubt their relationship with the US. "Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in the world, and a mere 28% of Australians trust China to do the same," says Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute, citing their annual poll. "Those are striking findings when you consider the level of trust that the Australian government has with the United States." The 'frenemy' While Australia's alliance with the US is changing, so too is its relationship with China. Armed forces might be prepping for a potential military conflict but the fact remains China is Australia's most important economic partner. Australia and China have had diplomatic relations since 1972 but it was only in the early 2010s that China became Australia's biggest trading partner, hungry for all the commodities it had to offer. Australia opened up its economy and encouraged business and trade, Chinese President Xi Jinping was invited to address parliament. And it culminated in the signing of a free trade agreement in 2015. The golden era didn't last long though. When Australia suggested an investigation into the origins of Covid in 2020, China objected to this line of questioning and retaliated with tariffs. And then in 2021, Australia became the first nation to perform a U-turn on China's Belt and Road Initiative - its massive global infrastructure plan - when they cancelled the state of Victoria's agreement with the Chinese government three years after signing up. A number of Australians have also been detained in China, including journalist Cheng Lei, who was released in 2023 after more than three years. Relations have improved in recent years under the Labor government of Anthony Albanese, but it's not without challenges. In June this year for example, China slapped 55% tariffs on beef to protect its own domestic market - despite the free trade agreement. Even with these hiccups, this year's Lowy Institute Poll found that a majority of Australians (61%) saw China more as an economic partner than a security threat. That was an 11-point increase from last year. When it comes to China investing in Australia though, they are more wary. "There are a number of European countries which are larger investors in Australia than China, and that is because our jurisdictions are much more similar, and there is a greater level of trust between our governments," says Lyons-Jones. This year's Lowy Institute Poll also showed that for the first time, a majority of Australians (51%) believed that Australia's relationship with China was more important than its relationship with the US. Rise and fall of superpowers Earlier this month, former Prime Minister Kevin Rudd – a fluent Mandarin speaker - gave an address in which he talked of "radical changes" now reshaping Australia's national security, including "the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be". Dr Marina Yue Zhang, an Associate Professor at the University of Technology Sydney agrees Australia's relationship with its closest ally is changing. "The US is really doing something dramatic and more and more people in Australia - and I think globally - have realised 'is this the big brother we can all trust and put all our faith in?' " she says. But old rivalries live on. With Australia caught between two superpowers, every exchange between their leaders carries weight. And in Beijing earlier this year, when Xi met Trump, the Chinese president invoked the idea of the "Thucydides Trap", the theory that conflict can become almost inevitable when a rising power challenges an established one. "This is, if not the transition of great powers, at least [it's] power struggles of great powers, says Zhang. And in that competition, Australia is inevitably affected. The US is a security ally that while more unreliable than in the past is still its mainstay. But economically so too is China. It's not an either/or relationship, it's a balancing act. "There's no way Australia will choose one side and [dump] the other- it's not in their interests," Zhang says. "It's getting harder and harder to maintain, but Australia has to do it."

item.title: Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m27dprvzv7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far - Published Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months. The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police. Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer. The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa. Here's what we know. Busisiwe Mahlangu Case 1 Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties. Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed. Itumeleng Kekana Case 2 Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026. The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park. No arrests have been made so far. Nomfesane Mjobo Case 3 Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park. Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises. No arrests have been made. Unknown woman Case 4 Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear. No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made. Gracious Nkomo Case 5 Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area. Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death. Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo Case 6 Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park. Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case. Unidentified woman Case 7 Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed. No arrests have been made. Dineo Motapane Case 8 The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive. Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni. She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case. Jabulile Ntimba Case 9 The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni. According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence. The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice. Ntombifuthi Nxumalo Case 10 The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body. This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death. A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge. Unidentified woman Case 11 The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni. The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area. The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared. No arrests have been made. Boitumelo Gift Mashita Case 12 Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken. Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand. Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies. While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September. The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg. It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni. President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience". South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone. South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day. Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests. item.title: How an alleged rape sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostels
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6kg8dxrv54do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How an alleged rape sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostels - Published One of India's largest private universities has suspended classes after an unverified allegation that a female student was raped on campus set off protests that descended into violence. Police say they have registered a case and are trying to verify whether last week's alleged rape at Lovely Professional University (LPU) did happen. The university has categorically denied the allegation. Police say no student has come forward to say she was assaulted, investigators have yet to identify the alleged victim or the perpetrator, and CCTV footage examined so far has yielded no evidence of an attack. But rumours on student WhatsApp groups led to unrest over the weekend at the sprawling 600-acre university in Punjab that draws students from India and abroad. Founded in 2005 by a family whose business began with a small sweet shop, LPU has grown into a largely self-contained world of hostels and lecture halls, with thousands of young people living on campus. Images and videos showed vehicles in flames, crowds filling a major highway and police wielding canes as unrest spilled beyond the university gates. Police vehicles were damaged, officers injured and parts of the campus was vandalised. By Monday, the highway had reopened and the campus was calmer, but heavily policed. University authorities described the claims circulating on social media as false and baseless, but it did little to reassure students with hostels emptying within hours. Key exams were postponed and students were allowed to go home. Following demands from protesting students, police registered a rape case against "an unidentified person" and formed a seven-member special investigation team, or SIT, to investigate. What happened? The unrest began in the early hours of 27 September, when word spread that a female student had been raped in or near one of the university's hostels a few days earlier. The suspect was variously described - by students and in media reports - as a plumber, painter or construction worker. Some students said the assault had occurred on 23 September and accused the university of failing to act after being informed. BBC Punjabi found that messages about the allegation had circulated through WhatsApp groups. As they travelled, crowds gathered. Hundreds eventually spilled on to National Highway 44, a major route between Delhi and Punjab, blocking traffic for more than 15 hours. By Sunday evening, university property had been damaged, objects set alight and stones thrown at police vehicles. Videos showed police striking protesters with canes, although police later denied carrying out a baton-charge. Behind the gates, students described a night of fear. "We were sitting with knives and scissors," Arya, a student, told BBC Punjabi. Students had been told to lock themselves inside their rooms, she said, while people knocked on their doors. "We were just thinking that somehow this night would pass and we would get out of here." Police later arrived and made them feel safer, she said. By the next day, she wanted to leave. "Our parents also want us to just get out of here." So why have police lodged a case? That the police open a case and investigate the allegation was among the protesters' central demands. "The students have been demanding that an FIR [First Information Report] is to be registered, but the students could not provide us with any victim's name," senior police official Naveen Singla told the BBC. Police nevertheless registered an FIR under India's rape law against an unidentified person. An FIR formally records an allegation for investigation; it does not establish that a crime occurred. Singla said investigators had also begun examining CCTV footage. The preliminary search, he told the BBC, had so far shown no outsider entering a room. "As of now, it can't be verified that rape has happened or not," he said. But they are continuing to examine the footage. "The campus is quite large, so we haven't been able to see all the cameras yet," Sinha told reporters on Monday. "We have initially checked the places that the students had mentioned, but we will get to the bottom of this." Why did the protests grow so large? It is difficult to say. What began with an allegation of rape quickly became a broader protest over security, the university's response and, eventually, the violence itself. There was also growing uncertainty over who was on the campus. Some students insisted the demonstrations had begun peacefully and blamed outsiders for at least some of the violence. Others told BBC Punjabi of seeing masked or unfamiliar people inside the university. "We were really scared," said Pawan, a student. "It became a complete battlefield." Another student, Aniket Singh, said outsiders had entered a women's hostel and knocked on doors claiming to be police officers. Police have since confirmed that outsiders were among the crowds, but said they were still trying to establish who they were and what role they played. Amid that confusion, the university's attempt to dispel the rape allegation produced a controversy of its own. On Monday, LPU released a video of three women living in the hostel room that had been linked to the alleged assault. They said nothing had happened there and asked people to stop disturbing them. The same students later alleged in another video that university officials had instructed them what to say, edited the recording and posted it without their consent. Those claims have not been independently verified. LPU has not commented on the students' allegations. Another claim circulating during the protests sought to connect the alleged rape with the recent suicide of a female LPU student from Telangana state. Police say investigations into her death had already begun and there is no verified evidence linking the two cases. What is happening now? For now, life on campus has been interrupted. Regular classes have been suspended for 10 days and exams postponed. Students have been asked to return home after consulting their parents or guardians. Those who are staying have been advised to stay in their residences and avoid further unrest. The Punjab State Women's Commission has also sought the FIR, details of the investigation and information about arrangements for students' safety. The investigation now has two separate questions to answer: whether there is evidence of the assault that set the protests in motion? And who was responsible for the violence that followed? Addressing the students on Monday, LPU's pro-chancellor Rashmi Mittal said she was hurt that despite the university's many channels for students to raise concerns, they had instead "believed the rumour that was spreading". She also alleged that outsiders had joined the unrest. "I feel students can't do this," she said. item.title: Sign before praying: A new conversion law is affecting churchgoers in Indian state
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmj4jg2vxvpdo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Sign before praying: A new conversion law is affecting churchgoers in Indian state - Published Some churches in and around India's financial capital Mumbai have begun asking worshippers to give a declaration in writing - "I came here to pray of my own free will." Visitors write down their names, sometimes add an ID card number, and sign to say that nobody forced or enticed them to attend church. The forms, a copy of which the BBC has seen, have no official standing. Churches keep them in case a prayer meeting is challenged and its organisers are accused of trying to convert those inside. The practice began at some churches in late August, just before a new law against religious conversion took effect in Maharashtra state, of which Mumbai is the capital. The law prohibits religious conversions brought about by force, fraud, coercion or inducement. It also requires people who want to convert voluntarily to notify authorities in advance. An unlawful conversion can lead to a prison sentence of up to seven years, rising to 10 for a repeat offence. Maharashtra's government says the law protects people, particularly those who are socially or economically vulnerable, from being forced or deceived into changing their religion. But critics say its broad definitions, severe penalties and scrutiny of even voluntary conversions risk drawing the state and the police into one of the most private decisions a person can make. The state government did not respond to the BBC's repeated requests for comment. While the law applies to all religions, the anxiety is being felt most deeply at places where minorities, especially Christians, worship. At the heart of the debate is a long-running tension over allegations, usually made by right-wing groups, about people being coerced or induced to change their religion for benefits. Devdan Tribhuvan has seen some of that anxiety up close. A fourth-generation Christian, he is part of an organisation that provides legal aid to the community in Mumbai. In recent months, he says, people have increasingly approached him not about court cases, but with accounts of disrupted prayer meetings and questions about what they are still free to do. Some have described strangers walking into churches and questioning those inside: "What is your name? Why are you here? Has anyone offered you something?" The questions can become more pointed, Tribhuvan said, when a worshipper has a name that does not sound Christian: "Has anyone forced you to come? Has anyone offered you an inducement?" Many who contact him are not looking to take legal action. They want to know whether simply gathering to pray could leave them vulnerable to an accusation of conversion. In July, an investigation by The Indian Express, external documented five disruptions of Christian prayer meetings around Mumbai between April and July. Nine police cases followed - seven against worshippers or prayer organisers, and two against members of the Hindu nationalist group Bajrang Dal. Police did not respond to detailed questions about the cases or the action taken. "Is gathering for prayer itself conversion?" Tribhuvan asks. In Mumbai, Tribhuvan's question carries particular weight. The city grew by drawing people from across India and beyond, bringing their gods and rituals with them. A church bell can sound within earshot of a mosque's call to prayer; a shrine belonging to one faith can draw followers of another. People of many faiths make their way to the Muslim shrine Haji Ali. Hindus light candles at Mount Mary, a Catholic basilica overlooking the city. Crowds fill the streets around Lalbaug during the Hindu festival of Ganesh Chaturthi and stream to Siddhivinayak temple throughout the year. Maharashtra is the latest of more than a dozen states to restrict religious conversion. The laws differ, but their reach has expanded in recent years, particularly in states governed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party. Several are being challenged before the Supreme Court. Behind that expansion lie claims long made by Hindu nationalist groups, that Christians use money, schooling or medical care to draw poor and tribal communities away from Hinduism, and that Muslim men court Hindu women to convert them - an alleged conspiracy they call "love jihad." Critics say such accusations have fuelled harassment of Christian prayer meetings and interfaith couples, and that the laws give those making them a way to draw the police into questions of prayer, marriage and belief. Maharashtra's government says the new law leaves people free to convert by choice, while addressing what it says is a rise in forced conversions that existing laws have failed to curb. Critics question where it draws the line between force and choice. "We do not support forceful conversions, if any," said Samsuddin Tamboli, president of the Muslim Satyashodhak Mandal (Muslim Truth-seeking Society), a reformist organisation. His concern is what the law counts as inducement. Its definition of "allurement" includes employment, free education at a religious institution, a promise of marriage, a "better lifestyle" and "divine healing". Even glorifying one religion over another can fall within it. "The definition has been kept so vague that almost any benefit accruing to a person can be considered or argued to be an allurement," said Abhay Thipsay, a retired Bombay High Court judge. "If a person receives some benefit and consciously chooses to convert for that reason, why should it be considered wrong?" The law also allows parents, siblings and other relatives to complain to police about an allegedly unlawful conversion, leaving the person accused of causing or assisting it to prove that it was lawful. Critics say for interfaith couples, that provision adds another potential obstacle to marriages that can already face family opposition. Indian law allows people of different faiths to marry without converting, but requires a month's notice. Lara Jesani, a lawyer who has helped interfaith couples obtain court protection, said details of planned weddings have sometimes reached relatives and Hindu nationalist groups opposed to them within that notice period. In cases she has handled, she said, families have taken women away, even from the marriage registrar's office. Now, she fears the new law may give the families or right-wing organisations a new way to target such couples. "Even when neither intend to convert, [the couples] fear a relative could accuse one partner of trying to convert the other." The Maharashtra government did not respond to detailed questions from the BBC about these concerns. But when the law was passed, state minister Pankaj Bhoyar said it did not infringe upon the right to change religion. The notification requirement, he said, was intended to establish whether a conversion was voluntary, while allowing the state to act against those brought about by fraud, coercion or inducement. But Tribhuvan is still worried, an anxiety, he says, which reaches even the small prayer gatherings held closer to home when a church is too far away. Fifty people might attend, he said, sometimes 100 - and someone who is not Christian might join too. "If someone else wishes to come and pray, we cannot stop them," he said. "That is what we call the right to choose." To Thipsay, the retired judge, the precaution points to a larger question. "If an adult has the power to make major decisions - such as whom to marry - and has been given the right to vote," he said, "why should they not have the power to make this decision too?"

========================================
Watch: From launch to fiery splashdown, SpaceX's Starship completes orbit test SpaceX's Starship rocket has splashed down in the Pacific Ocean after orbiting the Earth for about three hours. The mission was supposed to last about 10 hours, but the SpaceX team decided to end it early. The ship deployed 26 "next generation" Starlink V3 satellites, joining the existing constellation which deliver broadband internet on Earth. SpaceX describes Starship as "the world's most powerful launch vehicle ever developed" and says it will eventually carry crew and cargo "to Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars and beyond". The aim of the spacecraft is to be able to carry up to 100 people on "long-duration, inter-planetary flights".
